discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.
How do you decide what to eat?

Do you think your gender influences what you eat? Tell us more about
why or why not.

Imagine you decided to go plant-based — what would need to change in
your life for you to do that?

What might make plant-based foods more appealing to you or other men
you know?

Okay everyone, that’s our time. Thanks so much for participating
today. Before we finish, is there anything else you would like to add
about food choices, gender, masculinity, or plant-based eating?

mm_fg1_amir.name: Amir
mm_fg1_amir.profile_summary: Amir, 20, Male. Urban, West Midlands, UK. Meat eater.

masculine_norms.construct: Traditional masculinity norms measured with the Male Role Norms Inventory (MRNI; Levant et al., 1992), subscales: avoidance of femininity, restrictive emotionality, aggression, achievement status, self-reliance, and attitudes toward sex (54 items; homophobia subscale excluded).
masculine_norms.direction: Higher scores indicate stronger endorsement of traditional masculine norms.

masculinity_of_meat.construct: Perceived masculinity of meat measured with the 7-item Masculinity of Meat scale (Lax & Mertig, 2020; e.g. 'Men need to eat meat more than women do').
masculinity_of_meat.direction: Higher scores indicate stronger perceived masculinity-meat link and anti-vegetarian bias.

meat_attachment.construct: Meat attachment measured with a 5-item shortened form of the Meat Attachment Questionnaire (Graça et al., 2015; e.g. 'Meat is irreplaceable in my diet').
meat_attachment.direction: Higher scores indicate stronger emotional and habitual attachment to eating meat.

dairy_attachment.construct: Dairy attachment measured on an identical scale to meat attachment, with 'dairy' replacing 'meat' (Graça et al., 2015 adaptation).
dairy_attachment.direction: Higher scores indicate stronger emotional and habitual attachment to dairy consumption.

vegetarianism_threat.construct: Perceived threat from the rise of vegetarianism measured with the 8-item Vegetarianism Threat Scale (Dhont & Hodson, 2014; e.g. 'The rise of vegetarianism poses a threat to our country’s cultural customs').
vegetarianism_threat.direction: Higher scores indicate stronger perceived societal or cultural threat from vegetarianism.
vegetarianism_threat.rescaling_note: Values in the dataset appear rescaled from the original 1–5 to 1–7 range, likely for comparability with other constructs.

simulation_config.notes: Recruited as a regular meat eater. Survey profile: traditional masculinity norms 4.0/7 (moderate); perceived masculinity-meat link 5.0/7 (above-average); meat attachment 5.0/7 (above-average); dairy attachment 4.4/7 (moderate); vegetarianism threat 3.0/7 (below-average).
